A courtyard is an outdoor, open-to-the-sky space that is enclosed — fully or partially — by the walls of a building or by a group of buildings around it.

Think of it this way: imagine a building shaped like a square doughnut. The hole in the middle — that open area surrounded by the building on all four sides — is a courtyard.

Two things define a courtyard:

  1. It is outdoors — it has no roof; the sky is above it.
  2. It is enclosed — walls or buildings wrap around it on most or all sides.

Without the enclosure, it's just an open field. Without being outdoors, it becomes a hall or a room. The combination of being outside and being enclosed is what makes something a courtyard.

A courtyard can be big or small. The ground is usually paved with stone, brick, or tiles — though it can also have grass, gravel, or soil. Many courtyards are simple and plain. Others are beautifully decorated, with a fountain at the center, potted plants along the edges, benches to sit on, trees for shade, or flower beds. Some have covered walkways called arcades or colonnades running along the inner walls, so people can walk around the courtyard while staying sheltered from rain.

You can find courtyards in many kinds of buildings and places:

  • Homes and mansions — especially large, traditional homes. In India, the central open space inside a haveli is a classic courtyard. In Spanish and Latin American homes, it is called a patio (though the two words are related but slightly different — more on that below).
  • Palaces and castles — large royal buildings almost always had one or more courtyards. Knights trained there; ceremonies were held there.
  • Universities and schools — many old universities (like Oxford or Cambridge) are built around courtyards, which students and professors cross when moving between buildings.
  • Religious buildings — mosques, temples, churches, and monasteries often have a courtyard where people gather before or after prayer.
  • Hotels — many hotels, especially heritage and boutique hotels, are built around a central courtyard that serves as a quiet, scenic common area.
  • Government buildings, museums, and historical monuments — grand public buildings frequently have inner courtyards.

A courtyard serves several purposes, both practical and social:

  • Light and air — Before electricity and air conditioning, rooms facing an inner courtyard got natural light and a breeze. A building could have windows or doorways opening onto the courtyard, making the interiors liveable.
  • Privacy — Because a courtyard is enclosed, it is a protected, semi-private outdoor space. People inside can enjoy fresh air without being exposed to the street or public.
  • Gathering and socializing — Courtyards are natural meeting points. Family members, students, residents, or workers naturally collect in the shared open space. Meals, conversations, celebrations, and markets have all taken place in courtyards throughout history.
  • Safety — In medieval times, people kept livestock in courtyards at night for protection, and soldiers could defend a castle's courtyard as a last resort.
  • Beauty and calm — A well-designed courtyard with a fountain, plants, and shade provides a peaceful retreat from noise and activity.

The enclosure is not just a physical feature — it changes the experience of the space. A courtyard feels sheltered and intimate, almost like an outdoor room. The walls block wind, reduce noise from outside, and create a sense of belonging to the place. This is why courtyards have been built across every culture and every era: they offer the benefits of being outside while maintaining the comfort of feeling enclosed and protected.
How a courtyard differs from similar words

These words are related but mean different things:

  • Yard — A yard is simply the open land around a building. It does not need to be enclosed. Your front yard or backyard is open on at least one side and blends into the surroundings. A courtyard is specifically enclosed.
  • Garden — A garden is defined by its content — it is a place where plants, flowers, or vegetables are grown. A courtyard is defined by its shape and position — enclosed by buildings. A courtyard can have a garden in it, but a garden by itself is not a courtyard.
  • Patio — A patio is a paved outdoor area directly attached to a house, usually at the back or side, meant for relaxing, dining, or socializing. A patio is generally not enclosed by walls on multiple sides the way a courtyard is. It is usually open on at least two or three sides. A patio is smaller and more personal; a courtyard implies more enclosure and often a grander or more formal structure.
  • Atrium — In ancient Roman homes, an atrium was an open courtyard near the entrance of the house. Today, the word "atrium" is used for a large, tall, covered indoor space in modern buildings (like a shopping mall or an airport), often with a glass roof. So modern atriums are indoors, while courtyards are always outdoors.
  • Cloister — A cloister is a specific type of courtyard found in monasteries and convents. It is typically a rectangular garden surrounded by a covered walkway on all four sides. A cloister is a kind of courtyard, but with specific religious and architectural associations.
  • Plaza / Square — These are large open public spaces in a town or city. They are not enclosed by a single building. A courtyard belongs to a specific building or complex; a plaza or square belongs to the public.

If you have ever walked through a narrow street and then stepped through an arched doorway into a quiet, open space with a fountain and trees, surrounded by old walls — that sudden shift from noise to calm, from narrow to open, from public to private — that is the distinctive experience of a courtyard. It is one of the oldest and most universal designs in human architecture precisely because it delivers this feeling so reliably.

• The children played in the courtyard while the adults sat under the arches nearby.
  • The old university was built around a central courtyard with a large lawn and stone paths.
  • From the hotel room, she could look down into the courtyard below, where a fountain was running quietly.
  • The soldiers gathered in the castle courtyard at dawn.
  • Many rooms in the haveli opened directly onto the inner courtyard, keeping the home cool in summer.

A courtyard is an open, outdoor, unroofed space enclosed by the walls of buildings around it. It brings together two things that seem like opposites — the openness of the outdoors and the enclosure of a building — to create a space that is sheltered, private, and often beautiful. You find courtyards in homes, palaces, schools, mosques, hotels, and countless other buildings across the world and throughout history.
